column5: Book dates the Atlantic expedition to 1312 and calls the Mansa's predecessor his uncle who named Kankan Musa heir; says records indicate some reached the Americas. Course says c.1311 and unproven. Arabic source (al-Umari, via Musa's own account in Cairo) gives the predecessor's 400-ship then 2,000-ship voyages without a kinship claim to Musa and no landfall. Trust al-Umari; book's 'reached the Americas' is unsupported; 1312 vs c.1311 is a dating discrepancy to show side by side.

Popular framing of the ship story (400 ships then 2,000, one ship returned and reported a river-like current at sea) matches the al-Umari report structure; book adds invented scene on the beach. Use only the structure, label scene as the author's dramatisation.

Ebony throne with ivory tusks, palace at Niani, umbrella, herald and the bandit-clearing and gold-miner 'pagan customs' episode are given with no source in the text. Not in al-Umari, Ibn Battuta or Ibn Khaldun as cited in the course. Do not teach as fact; may be used as a labelled example of unsourced popular detail.

Dyeli (griot) described as counsellor, herald and keeper of epic, low-status by design so dependent on the ruler. Course Module 1 lesson 2 treats griots as structured historians; extends with the political-independence reason (no kin among nobility). Book gives no source; treat as popular explanation, label.

Chapter titled 'A reality-based imaginary day': market day in Niani is an explicit imaginative reconstruction. Mentions 10,000-strong cavalry (cf al-Umari's figures for the army), imported Arab/Barb horses too expensive, kola, state monopoly on strategic imports (note 4). Good worked example of a popular text mixing fiction with source; do not cite as evidence.

Salt from Taghaza traded south for Wangara gold, a donkey-for-camel-for-porter transfer chain, tsetse limiting pack animals, taxes at 'port' towns. Book says general rate was ounce of gold for ounce of salt; this rate is not attested in the Arabic sources I can check (Ibn Battuta describes salt used as currency and Taghaza slabs but no 1:1 gold rate). Flag the 1:1 rate as unsupported; use the transport chain as extension to Module 3 trans-Saharan table.

Olivier, a popular young-readers book, gives: 60,000 followers (cf course: figures vary), 8,000 soldiers from an army of 100,000, 500 gold-staff bearers, 80 camels carrying 300 lb each (24,000 lb), Cairo sojourn three months, gold price depressed for 'more than twelve years' (al-Umari: gold price in Cairo fell and stayed low; course says 'for years'), return with as-Sahili and four sharifs. Several details appear to follow al-Umari/Ibn Khaldun; the 80 camel loads of 300 lb is NOT in the sources I can check. Course already says numbers vary; keep the lesson caution and cite Olivier as an example of one popular rendering.

Book says Mansa Musa and as-Sahili introduced sun-dried mud brick and the 'Malian style' to the Sudan. Course archaeology (Module 1 Jenne-jeno, walled town from first millennium CE; Module 2 Kerma mud-brick) shows mud brick long predates 1324. Trust archaeology; book's 'introduced mud brick' is a popular overstatement. At most as-Sahili brought a distinct architectural idiom (flat-roofed, stone/plaster audience hall): book itself places the plastered palace at Timbuktu; I cannot check against the Arabic sources here.

Book asserts Mansa Musa 'founded' the University of Sankore at Timbuktu with thousands of students. Course says only that he patronised mosque-building in Timbuktu and Gao. 'University' is a modern label for a cluster of mosque schools and the book gives no source. Keep course wording; teach 'university' as a later and contested label. Not verified against Hunwick's Timbuktu sources (not ingested).

Book claims Mali's copper fed Ife (1000s) and Benin (1300s) bronze sculpture. Course Module 5 dates Ife heads c.12th to 15th centuries and Benin plaques to the 16th and 17th centuries; the 1000s date for Ife and 'Mali copper' supply have no support here. Reject as unsupported; refer to Module 5.

Book says Musa ran out of gold in Cairo and borrowed at a rate of 700 dinars for every 300 borrowed (note 10); Catalan Atlas (1375) drawn from Jewish informants; Dulcert chart 15 years after the pilgrimage. Course l2 only says gold lowered Cairo price and Catalan Atlas shows him with a nugget. The borrowing and interest figures are an extension; plausible as an al-Umari-derived report but I cannot check the cited note (note 10) here; label as reported, not firm.

Book narrates Mansa Musa receiving the submission of Gao and the Songhai king, taking two princes as hostages, after learning of a Mali victory while returning; Epilogue says the two princes later escaped, one reigned at Gao, and Songhai broke away. This is a single narrative; the course does not cover Gao's incorporation. Chronology is uncertain (some sources put Gao's capture before the pilgrimage); mark [CONTESTED] if used. Anachronism: 'Songhai kingdom' of the 1320s is not the later empire.

Book describes Mali's administration: village chiefs, city inspectors, provincial governors, conquered states ruled by own leaders paying tribute and troops, resident representatives, paid bureaucracy; calls Mali the second largest empire in the world and the size of Western Europe combined. Structure is a useful summary for Module 4 / comparison with Diop's analysis (political organisation chapters); the size and rank superlatives are unsupported.

Musa died 1337; reign 'increased contact with Egypt'; secrecy about gold source via the 'gold grows like plants' story told when pressed by a polite listener. Matches the course's caution that Musa's gold claims come through Cairo hearsay. The gold-plant withering detail is not independently attested in the text; note as a story, not evidence. Also 'Maghan ruled four years then Sulayman Musa' fits the course's Mansa Suleyman king since 1341 (1337 + 4).

Chapter closes by naming its sources (Mali epic, Timbuktu manuscripts, al-Umari, archaeology). Epilogue: Mossi burned Timbuktu in Maghan's reign; end of Golden Age at Sulayman's death; Songhai replaced Mali. Claim that Malian living standards were 'comparable to or better than contemporary Europe' (note 15) is unsupported and non-comparable; do not teach.

column4: ch-002 and ch-021 (note 2, Glossary 'Canoes and Ships')
column5: Book backs the Atlantic-crossing idea with Van Sertima (They Came Before Columbus) and the claim that Abu Bakari II 'almost certainly' left from Dakar and drifted to the New World. Course says Atlantic voyages from Mali are unproven and Mande-American contact is [CONTESTED], rejected by most archaeologists. Keep the course position; show the book as a popular source that treats it as likely, and say the only evidence for the voyages themselves is al-Umari's report of Mansa Musa's own account.

Author states he combined sources, made the predecessor an uncle although the relationship is uncertain (uncle vs cousin; matrilineal succession), attributed two Ibn Battuta observations to Musa, and added invented details and dialogue ('responsible imagining') for young readers. This is the key evidence for treating the book as a retelling, not a source. Confirms the course's source-distance method. Also reveals dating uncertainty: glossary gives the reign as 1307-1332 or 1312-1337.

Glossary supplies names the course lacks: Abu Bakari II (the Voyager King), the Egyptian merchant Saraj al-Din ibn al-Kuwayk (lender of the 700-for-300 loan; his son collected from Mali), the general Sagmandir, Ali Koleni and Sulayman Nar (the Songhai princes), Wangara probably Bambuk and maybe Bure, Takedda copper rods; a cited estimate that one-third of Musa's caravan died (Cambridge History of Africa, not seen); slavery gloss relying on Davidson (people moved up and down easily). The slavery gloss is a one-sided popular claim; compare with Module 8 and Rodney.

Book is a young-readers retelling (author surname printed Oliver on the cover; the brief writes Olivier). Its bibliography is mostly secondary and popular (Davidson, Levtzion, Time-Life, Van Sertima); it cites no Arabic text directly. Use for al-Umari cross-check only where the notes point to Levtzion; never as evidence. Also: the Author's Note says women are underrepresented because the Arabic authors were male and from North Africa; Ibn Battuta's surprise at Walata women's freedom fits Module 4 Ibn Battuta lesson.
